claim: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) affects 1 in 4000 people worldwide.
source: Retinitis Pigmentosa (RP) is a disease of the retina that affects 1 in 4000 people worldwide (Hartong et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hartong et al., 2006

claim: RP is characterized by an initial loss of night vision, followed by loss of color and daylight vision.
source: It is characterized by an initial loss of night vision, followed by loss of color and daylight vision.
evidence: Supported by established clinical knowledge about RP progression

claim: A typical patient with RP loses night vision as an adolescent and subsequently loses central daylight vision by the age of 60.
source: Although the disease progression is variable, a typical patient with RP loses night vision as an adolescent and subsequently loses central daylight vision by the age of 60 (Hartong et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hartong et al., 2006

claim: Over 65 causative genes for RP have been identified.
source: Although gene therapy via gene augmentation has proven to be effective in humans (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Cideciyan et al., 2008; Hauswirth et al., 2008; Maguire et al., 2008), a one-by-one genetic augmentation approach is currently not feasible given that over 65 causative genes for RP have been identified (RetNet).
evidence: Supported by citation to RetNet database

claim: Gene therapy via gene augmentation has proven to be effective in humans for RP.
source: Although gene therapy via gene augmentation has proven to be effective in humans (Bainbridge et al., 2008; Cideciyan et al., 2008; Hauswirth et al., 2008; Maguire et al., 2008), a one-by-one genetic augmentation approach is currently not feasible given that over 65 causative genes for RP have been identified (RetNet).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies

claim: Many RP patients have a disease gene that is expressed solely in rods, causing rod dysfunction and death.
source: Many RP patients have a disease gene that is expressed solely in rods, causing rod dysfunction and death (Cideciyan et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cideciyan et al., 1998

claim: Cones suffer from bystander effects in RP, leading to poor daylight and color vision.
source: Cones then suffer from bystander effects, leading to poor daylight and color vision, and in many cases, complete blindness.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of secondary cone degeneration in RP

claim: In animal models of RP, cones in the far periphery survive even in the absence of surviving rods.
source: Intriguingly, we and others have noted that, in animal models of RP, the cones in the far periphery survive, even in the absence of surviving rods (Cideciyan et al., 1998; Carter-Dawson et al., 1978; Charng et al., 2016; García-Ayuso et al., 2013; García-Fernández et al., 1995; Jiménez et al., 1996; LaVail et al., 1997; Lin et al., 2009; Ma et al., 1998; Milam et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous studies

claim: Dark rearing can slow photoreceptor degeneration but does not rescue the degeneration phenotype.
source: However, while dark rearing can slow photoreceptor degeneration, particularly in albino RP animal models, it does not rescue the degeneration phenotype (Chang et al., 2007; Fan et al., 2005; Naash, 1996; Pang et al., 2008; Paskowitz et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to experimental studies

claim: Cone survival in the far periphery is confined to an area demarcated by a sharp boundary.
source: Additionally, cone survival in the far periphery is confined to an area demarcated by a sharp boundary, as opposed to a gradient, which would be expected if light exposure was the sole explanation.
evidence: Based on observation and logical inference from the pattern of cone survival

claim: The rd1 mouse harbors a viral insertion and a point mutation in the Pde6b gene.
source: It harbors a viral insertion and a point mutation in the Pde6b gene (Han et al., 2013), which is expressed only in rods.
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2013

claim: Pde6b is expressed only in rods.
source: It harbors a viral insertion and a point mutation in the Pde6b gene (Han et al., 2013), which is expressed only in rods.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge and citation

claim: Degeneration of rod photoreceptors in rd1 mice starts at approximately postnatal day 11 (P11).
source: Degeneration of rod photoreceptors starts at approximately postnatal day 11 (P11), and rapidly progresses, such that most rods degenerate by P20.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of rd1 mouse model

claim: Most rods in rd1 mice degenerate by P20.
source: Degeneration of rod photoreceptors starts at approximately postnatal day 11 (P11), and rapidly progresses, such that most rods degenerate by P20.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of rd1 mouse model

claim: In rd1 mice, CAR+ cones were enriched in the peripheral retina at P40, with a preference towards the dorsal region.
source: In agreement with previous studies, we found that Cone Arrestin+ (CAR; also known as Arr3) cones were enriched in the peripheral retina at P40, with a preference towards the dorsal region (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: CAR+ cones in the dorsal periphery of rd1 mice persisted at least up to P366.
source: CAR+ cones in the dorsal periphery persisted at least up to P366, and interestingly, a nearly straight boundary demarcated the zone of survival (Figure 1C, left panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The peripheral retina of rd1 mice contained significantly more cones compared to the central retina.
source: Quantification of the number of cones in sampled peripheral and central regions showed that the peripheral retina contained significantly more cones compared to the central retina (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Long-term peripheral cone survival occurs in rd10 and Rho-/- mouse models.
source: In both rd10 and Rho-/- mouse models, cones survived long-term in the peripheral retina, with the same pattern as seen in rd1, persisting at least up to P366 and P531, respectively (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: No Nrl signal was found in dorsal rd10 retinal sections at P366.
source: To corroborate, we performed single molecule fluorescent in situ hybridization (smFISH) for Nrl, a marker of rods, and Arr3, a marker of cones, in dorsal rd10 retinal sections at P366. While Arr3+ cones were sparsely detected in the ONL, no Nrl signal was found (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Aldh1a1 was highly enriched in the peripheral samples compared to central samples in cone RNA sequencing.
source: Among the DE genes, we found that Aldh1a1 was highly enriched in the peripheral samples (Figure 1E), matching the previous data that it is expressed in dorsal MG (McCaffery et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 1E and citation

claim: Aldh1a1 is expressed in dorsal Muller glia.
source: Among the DE genes, we found that Aldh1a1 was highly enriched in the peripheral samples (Figure 1E), matching the previous data that it is expressed in dorsal MG (McCaffery et al., 1992).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCaffery et al., 1992

claim: Aldh1a1, Aldh1a2, and Aldh1a3 catalyze the synthesis of retinoic acid (RA).
source: Functionally, Aldh1a1, Aldh1a2, and Aldh1a3 catalyze the synthesis of RA (RA), a metabolite that, when bound to RA receptor (RAR), drives transcription of RA target genes from genomic RA response elements (RAREs) (Cunningham and Duester, 2015; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunningham and Duester, 2015

claim: RA, when bound to RA receptor (RAR), drives transcription of RA target genes from genomic RA response elements (RAREs).
source: Functionally, Aldh1a1, Aldh1a2, and Aldh1a3 catalyze the synthesis of RA (RA), a metabolite that, when bound to RA receptor (RAR), drives transcription of RA target genes from genomic RA response elements (RAREs) (Cunningham and Duester, 2015; Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunningham and Duester, 2015

claim: In P25 rd1 retinal sections, Aldh1a1 puncta were distributed throughout the radial dimension of the dorsal retina.
source: To validate the expression pattern of Aldh1a1, we performed smFISH for Aqp4, a pan MG marker, and Aldh1a1, in P25 rd1 retinal sections. In the central retina, Aldh1a1 signal was detected only at low levels. However, in the dorsal retina, Aldh1a1 puncta were distributed throughout the radial dimension of the retina, suggestive of an expression pattern in MG, as MG processes exhibit this widespread pattern (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by smFISH data shown in Figure 1G

claim: In RARE-LacZ mice, B-gal was mostly localized to cell bodies in the INL and processes spanning the retinal section.
source: In sections, B-gal was mostly localized to cell bodies in the INL and processes spanning the retinal section, reminiscent of MG morphology (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1H

claim: B-gal staining overlapped with Glutamine Synthetase, indicating that most cells with activated RA signaling were Muller glia.
source: Accordingly, B-gal staining overlapped with that of Glutamine Synthetase, an MG marker, indicating that most cells with activated RA signaling were MG, although not all peripheral MG were B-gal+.
evidence: Supported by IHC data showing colocalization

claim: In retinal flatmounts, the strongest B-gal activity was observed in the dorsal periphery, demarcated with a clear border.
source: In retinal flatmounts, the strongest B-gal activity was observed in the dorsal periphery, demarcated with a clear border, and weaker activity was found in the ventral periphery, as previously described (Luo et al., 2004; Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by LacZ staining data shown in Figure 1I and citation

claim: In rd1; RARE-lacZ mice, the spatial pattern of B-gal expression closely matched that of CAR+ cone survival at both P40 and P100.
source: In rd1; RARE-lacZ mice, the spatial pattern of B-gal expression closely matched that of CAR+ cone survival in rd1 mice, at both P40 and P100 (Figure 1J).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1J

claim: The relative expression level of Aldh1a1 was significantly reduced in retinas with CAG-CreER compared to control littermates without CAG-CreER.
source: As assessed by ddPCR of the retina, the relative expression level of Aldh1a1 was significantly reduced in retinas with CAG-CreER, compared to control littermates without CAG-CreER (Mean ± SD: -CreER: 0.01203 ± 0.005;+ CreER: 0.0003 ± 0.0002) (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2B

claim: In P60 Aldh flox retinal flatmounts with CAG-CreER, there were fewer cones in the periphery compared to those without CAG-CreER.
source: In P60 Aldh flox retinal flatmounts without CAG-CreER, IHC for CAR showed abundant cone survival in the periphery. In contrast, those with CAG-CreER appeared to have fewer cones in the periphery (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Quantification of CAR+ cones in sampled dorsal regions showed a significant reduction in the number of cones in Aldh Flox mice with CAG-CreER.
source: Accordingly, quantification of CAR+ cones in sampled dorsal regions showed a significant reduction in the number of cones (Mean ± SD: -CreER: 40.94 ± 13.51;+ CreER: 23.9 ± 12.74), suggesting that RA is necessary for the locally enriched peripheral cone survival (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E

claim: RA is necessary for the locally enriched peripheral cone survival.
source: Accordingly, quantification of CAR+ cones in sampled dorsal regions showed a significant reduction in the number of cones (Mean ± SD: -CreER: 40.94 ± 13.51;+ CreER: 23.9 ± 12.74), suggesting that RA is necessary for the locally enriched peripheral cone survival (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from conditional knockout experiments

claim: Pdgfra-Cre drives expression of Cre in Muller glia.
source: To overcome this issue, we generated another Aldh Flox mouse line with Pdgfra-Cre, which drives expression of Cre in MG (Roesch et al., 2008; Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by citation to Roesch et al., 2008 and validation data in Figure 2F

claim: Aldh1a1 was essentially depleted in the retinas of mice with Pdgfra-Cre, while it remained in the liver at high levels.
source: Using ddPCR, the number of transcripts for Aldh1a1 was quantified from the retina and the liver. While Aldh1a1 remained in the liver at high levels, it was essentially depleted in the retinas of mice with Pdgfra-Cre, indicating the specificity of the Cre line (Retina: Mean ± SD: -CreER: 0.0128 ± 0.001;+ CreER: 0.0005 ± 0.0001; Liver: Mean ± SD: -CreER: 0.5579 ± 0.6069;+ CreER: 0.3255 ± 0.1793) (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2G

claim: There was a significant reduction in the number of cones in the dorsal retina of mice with Pdgfra-Cre compared to controls.
source: We then quantified the number of CAR+ cones in the dorsal retina and found a significant reduction in the number of cones in the retinas with Pdgfra-Cre compared to controls (Mean ± SD: -CreER: 48.62 ± 10.77;+ CreER: 18.73 ± 7.44) (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2H

claim: MG-specific RA signaling is necessary for the excess cone survival in the periphery.
source: These results indicate that MG-specific RA signaling is necessary for the excess cone survival in the periphery.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from MG-specific conditional knockout

claim: Overexpression of Cyp26a1 significantly reduced the number of dorsal cones compared to GFP only controls.
source: In accord with the cKO data, overexpression of Cyp26a1 significantly reduced the number of dorsal cones compared to GFP only controls (Mean ± SD: GFP: 15.81 ± 8.369;+ CreER: 9.416 ± 6.564) (Figure 2J–K).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J-K

claim: RA is necessary for the excess cone survival seen in the periphery of the rd1 mouse model.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that RA is necessary for the excess cone survival seen in the periphery of the rd1 mouse model.
evidence: Supported by multiple loss-of-function experiments

claim: In the absence of RA, the RARa-RXR dimer, bound to genomic RAREs, represses downstream transcription.
source: Canonically, the RARa-RXR dimer, bound to genomic RAREs, represses downstream transcription in the absence of the RA ligand (Cunningham and Duester, 2015; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cunningham and Duester, 2015

claim: In the presence of RA, the RARa-RXR dimer recruits co-transcriptional activators and the transcriptional machinery, leading to transcription of downstream genes.
source: In the presence of RA, the dimer recruits co-transcriptional activators and the transcriptional machinery, leading to transcription of downstream genes.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of RA signaling

claim: The major downstream transcriptional target of RAR is Cyp26a1, which breaks down RA.
source: The RA signaling pathway is tightly regulated via a type of feedback inhibition, as the major downstream transcriptional target of RAR is Cyp26a1, which breaks down RA.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge of RA signaling feedback

claim: RARa-VP16 transactivator fusion protein constitutively activates downstream transcriptional targets, even in the absence of RA.
source: To overcome this issue, a RARa-VP16 transactivator fusion protein was developed previously, to constitutively activate downstream transcriptional targets, even in the absence of RA (Lipkin et al., 1996; Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lipkin et al., 1996

claim: When bpCAG-BFP was combined with CAG-RARa-VP16, a strong induction of B-gal and Cyp26a1 expression was observed.
source: In contrast, when bpCAG-BFP was combined with CAG-RARa-VP16, a strong induction of B-gal and Cyp26a1 expression was observed, indicative of transcription from RA signaling (Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by IHC and smFISH data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Within the electroporated patches that included CAG-RARa-VP16, a high density of cones was observed.
source: Within the electroporated patches that included CAG-RARa-VP16, a high density of cones was observed (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Quantification of cones in the electroporated region showed a significant increase in the RARa-VP16 group compared to controls.
source: Quantification of cones in the electroporated region showed a significant increase in the RARa-VP16 group compared to controls (Mean ± SD: BFP: 19.14 ± 4.589; RARa: 38.8 ± 6.261) (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Electroporation of the postnatal mouse retina results in expression of constructs only in late-born cell types, including rods, MG, bipolar cells, and amacrine cells, but not cones.
source: Of note, electroporation of the postnatal mouse retina results in expression of constructs only in late-born cell types of the retina, including rods, MG, bipolar cells, and amacrine cells, but not cones (Matsuda and Cepko, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Matsuda and Cepko, 2004

claim: The effect of RARa-VP16 on cone survival is non-cell autonomous with respect to cones.
source: Therefore, this effect on cone survival is not due to expression of the constructs within cones, that is, it is a non-cell autonomous effect on cones.
evidence: Based on inference from electroporation specificity

claim: The region of increased cone survival was confined to the electroporated patch, with a sharp boundary.
source: Furthermore, the region of increased cone survival was confined to the electroporated patch, with a sharp boundary, suggesting that the effect of RA signaling on cone survival is restricted locally.
evidence: Based on observation of spatial pattern

claim: Cone survival was significantly increased in the RARa-VP16 group compared to controls even at P100.
source: Nevertheless, cone survival was significantly increased in the RARa-VP16 group compared to controls even at P100 (Mean ± SD: BFP: 11.67 ± 9.388; RARa: 25.41 ± 11.58), indicating that this effect lasts over an extended period of time.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data at P100

claim: The surviving cones in RARa-VP16 electroporated retinas also expressed M-opsin.
source: To this end, IHC for M-opsin (Opn1mw) was carried out, which showed that the surviving cones also expressed M-opsin (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The surviving cones in the electroporated patch also expressed H2B-GFP from the Gnat2-based cone promoter.
source: The surviving cones in the electroporated patch also expressed H2B-GFP, suggesting that these cones were positive for Gnat2, a cone marker (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3G

claim: RA signaling leads to survival of cones, instead of simply upregulating the expression of CAR.
source: These results show that RA signaling leads to survival of cones, instead of simply upregulating the expression of CAR.
evidence: Supported by multiple marker validation experiments

claim: RA signaling during cone degeneration (after P20) is sufficient for cone survival.
source: With such a paradigm, a significant increase in the number of cones in the rtTA+ group compared to controls was observed (Mean ± SD: -rtTA: 14.25 ± 2.723;+ rtTA: 24 ± 9.412), indicating that RA signaling during cone degeneration, and after rod degeneration (after P20), is sufficient for cone survival (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by temporal control experiment data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Co-electroporation with Cralbp-Cre, but not Rho-Cre, showed significant increases in the number of cones compared to controls.
source: Co-electroporation with Cralbp-Cre, but not Rho-Cre, showed significant increases in the number of cones compared to controls (No Cre) (Mean ± SD: No Cre: 9.125 ± 3.22; Rho: 13.07 ± 7.175; Cralbp: 20.61 ± 9.048) (Figure 3I).
evidence: Supported by cell-type-specific expression data shown in Figure 3I

claim: Overexpression of RARa-VP16 in Pdgfra-Cre+ retinas increased the number of cones compared to controls without Cre.
source: Overexpression of RARa-VP16 in the Cre+ retinas increased the number of cones compared to controls without Cre (Mean ± SD: -Cre: 16.32 ± 3.681;+ Cre: 29.25 ± 10.79) (Figure 3J), in keeping with the results from Cralbp-Cre electroporation.
evidence: Supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3J

claim: RA signaling activation in MG during cone degeneration (> P20) is sufficient to promote cone survival in regions without endogenous RA synthesis.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that RA signaling activation in MG during cone degeneration (> P20) is sufficient to promote cone survival in regions without endogenous RA synthesis.
evidence: Supported by multiple gain-of-function experiments

claim: ALDH1A1 was significantly enriched in the peripheral human retina compared to the central retina.
source: As assessed by ddPCR, ALDH1A1 was significantly enriched in the peripheral retina (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by ddPCR data from human retinas shown in Figure 4

claim: Active retinoic acid (RA) signaling in peripheral Muller glia is necessary for the abnormally long survival of peripheral cones in rd1 mice.
source: Here, we found that active retinoic acid (RA) signaling in peripheral Muller glia is necessary for the abnormally long survival of these peripheral cones.
evidence: Supported by loss-of-function experimental data

claim: RA depletion by conditional knockout of RA synthesis enzymes abrogated the extended survival of peripheral cones.
source: RA depletion by conditional knockout of RA synthesis enzymes, or overexpression of an RA degradation enzyme, abrogated the extended survival of peripheral cones.
evidence: Supported by conditional knockout experimental data

claim: Overexpression of an RA degradation enzyme abrogated the extended survival of peripheral cones.
source: RA depletion by conditional knockout of RA synthesis enzymes, or overexpression of an RA degradation enzyme, abrogated the extended survival of peripheral cones.
evidence: Supported by Cyp26a1 overexpression experimental data

claim: Constitutive activation of RA signaling in the central retina promoted long-term cone survival.
source: Conversely, constitutive activation of RA signaling in the central retina promoted long-term cone survival.
evidence: Supported by RARa-VP16 overexpression experimental data

claim: RA signaling mediates the prolonged peripheral cone survival in the rd1 mouse model of retinal degeneration.
source: These results indicate that RA signaling mediates the prolonged peripheral cone survival in the rd1 mouse model of retinal degeneration, and provide a basis for a generic strategy for cone survival in the many diseases that lead to loss of cone-mediated vision.
evidence: Supported by combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function experimental data

claim: Peripheral MG express Aldh1a1, leading to active transcription of RA target genes.
source: We found that peripheral MG express Aldh1a1, leading to active transcription of RA target genes, and that the regions with active RA signaling closely matched those with surviving cones.
evidence: Supported by smFISH and RARE-LacZ reporter data

claim: The regions with active RA signaling closely matched those with surviving cones.
source: We found that peripheral MG express Aldh1a1, leading to active transcription of RA target genes, and that the regions with active RA signaling closely matched those with surviving cones.
evidence: Supported by spatial correlation of RARE-LacZ and cone survival patterns

claim: RA signaling is not activated directly in cones.
source: Importantly, RA signaling is not activated directly in cones; and therefore, the mechanism that promotes cone survival is non-cell autonomous with regards to cones.
evidence: Based on RARE-LacZ reporter expression pattern

claim: The mechanism that promotes cone survival by RA signaling is non-cell autonomous with regards to cones.
source: Importantly, RA signaling is not activated directly in cones; and therefore, the mechanism that promotes cone survival is non-cell autonomous with regards to cones.
evidence: Based on cell-type-specific expression and electroporation data

claim: RA signaling plays a role in maintaining the integrity of the blood-retina-barrier (BRB) in the zebrafish eye.
source: For example, RA signaling plays a role in maintaining the integrity of the blood-retina-barrier (BRB) in the zebrafish eye, and BRB leakage is associated with cone degeneration (Ivanova et al., 2019; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivanova et al., 2019 and Pollock et al., 2018

claim: BRB leakage is associated with cone degeneration.
source: For example, RA signaling plays a role in maintaining the integrity of the blood-retina-barrier (BRB) in the zebrafish eye, and BRB leakage is associated with cone degeneration (Ivanova et al., 2019; Pollock et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ivanova et al., 2019 and Pollock et al., 2018

claim: The human central retina is more susceptible to photoreceptor death compared to the peripheral retina in both RP and age-related macular degeneration (AMD).
source: The human central retina is more susceptible to photoreceptor death compared to the peripheral retina in both RP and age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Charng et al., 2016; Fleckenstein et al., 2021), and it remains unclear what molecular mechanisms underlie this difference.
evidence: Supported by citations to Charng et al., 2016 and Fleckenstein et al., 2021

claim: CYP26A1 is a marker of the human central retina with sustained expression from embryo into adulthood.
source: One of the markers of the human central retina is the sustained expression of CYP26A1 from embryo into adulthood (Peng et al., 2019; da Silva and Cepko, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Peng et al., 2019 and da Silva and Cepko, 2017

claim: Development of the high acuity area in the chick requires inhibition of RA signaling.
source: While the function of these genes with opposing functions is unknown in the human retina, development of the high acuity area in the chick, which lacks rods as does the human fovea, requires inhibition of RA signaling (da Silva and Cepko, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to da Silva and Cepko, 2017

claim: During mouse and chick retinal development, Aldh1a1 and Aldh1a3 are expressed in retinal progenitor cells (RPC) of the dorsal and ventral peripheral regions, respectively.
source: During mouse and chick retinal development, Aldh1a1 and Aldh1a3 are expressed in retinal progenitor cells (RPC) of the dorsal and ventral peripheral regions, respectively (McCaffery et al., 1992; Goto et al., 2018; Sen et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to McCaffery et al., 1992, Goto et al., 2018, and Sen et al., 2005

claim: RA signaling in the chick retina plays a role in retinal patterning.
source: RA signaling in the chick retina plays a role in retinal patterning, as it is required for the correct cellular composition of the chick high acuity area, while in the mouse retina, it influences the perioptic mesenchyme and choroidal vasculature, but not retinal patterning (Cammas et al., 2010; Dupé et al., 2003; Fan, 2003; Goto et al., 2018; Molotkov et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In the mouse retina, RA signaling influences the perioptic mesenchyme and choroidal vasculature, but not retinal patterning.
source: RA signaling in the chick retina plays a role in retinal patterning, as it is required for the correct cellular composition of the chick high acuity area, while in the mouse retina, it influences the perioptic mesenchyme and choroidal vasculature, but not retinal patterning (Cammas et al., 2010; Dupé et al., 2003; Fan, 2003; Goto et al., 2018; Molotkov et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Postnatally, ventral Aldh1a3 expression gradually disappears while dorsal Aldh1a1 expression persists in adult MG.
source: Postnatally, ventral Aldh1a3 expression gradually disappears while dorsal Aldh1a1 expression persists in adult MG.
evidence: Based on established expression patterns

claim: No overt retinal phenotype has been reported when Aldh1a1, 2, and 3 were conditionally deleted in the adult mouse.
source: However, no overt retinal phenotype has been reported when Aldh1a1, 2, and 3 were conditionally deleted in the adult mouse, bringing into question whether RA signaling has any function in the adult retina.
evidence: Based on review of literature

claim: Adult MG have many of the molecular and morphological features of developing RPCs.
source: As adult MG have many of the molecular and morphological features of developing RPCs (Jadhav et al., 2009), we speculate that dorsal RPC-specific Aldh1a1 expression persists into adult MG-specific expression as part of the dorsal peripheral RPC gene expression program.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jadhav et al., 2009

claim: RA is an important regulator of vasculogenesis and the development of the BRB.
source: As RA is an important regulator of vasculogenesis and the development of the BRB (Pawlikowski et al., 2019), and the main intra-retinal vasculature enters the retina via the ventral structure, the optic stalk (later the optic disc) (Hyatt et al., 1996), it might be the case that RA synthesis by ventral MG after development is somehow incompatible with the proper regulation of these activities.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pawlikowski et al., 2019

claim: The main intra-retinal vasculature enters the retina via the ventral structure, the optic stalk (later the optic disc).
source: As RA is an important regulator of vasculogenesis and the development of the BRB (Pawlikowski et al., 2019), and the main intra-retinal vasculature enters the retina via the ventral structure, the optic stalk (later the optic disc) (Hyatt et al., 1996), it might be the case that RA synthesis by ventral MG after development is somehow incompatible with the proper regulation of these activities.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hyatt et al., 1996
